blocks.html: To show clearly that this impostor du Tilh was attainted and convicted also of sacrilege, it must be understood that although of old the Gentiles and Pagans (who placed all their religion and hope, together with the greatness and majesty of their gods, in idols) thought that alone to be sacrilege which was stolen from the temples dedicated to the honour and service of their idols; and although some time afterwards, occasion being taken from this, sacrilege came to be properly referred to theft committed in Churches, or of sacred things a; nevertheless, by a larger interpretation, those who despised the gods were of old also called Sacrilegious. Thus Ovid, in some place, calls Lycurgus Sacrilegious, because he had despised the sacrifices of the god Bacchus. In the same way the Christians have generally called sacrilege every pollution and profanation of a sacred thing, every contempt and irreverence toward God, or toward the things instituted by him b: as for example, an abuse committed upon the sacrament of Baptism is rightly called Sacrilege c; so too a violence done to the Ministers of the Church d. Likewise a piece of magic, inasmuch as the magician abuses holy words in the invocation of spirits e. Thus he who traffics and makes merchandise of spiritual things is with good reason said to be Sacrilegious f; nay, he who disputes the power of the Prince, and calls into doubt whether the man whom he has chosen and called to his service is sufficient and worthy, deserves the title of Sacrilegious g. We read also that Sallust called Terentia, Cicero's wife, Sacrilegious h, because she was so troublesome, and so depraved in her manners, that Cicero, on his return from exile, was constrained to repudiate her i. Wherefore there is no doubt that those who despise, abuse and profane a thing so holy and sacred as marriage deserve to be called and judged Sacrilegious, and as such are worthy of death k, the ordinary penalty of the sacrilegious, who have been at all times so odious that the ancients at times burned them alive l. And although pity and compassion for age, in other crimes and even in this one, ought to incline the judges to some gentleness and moderation of penalty m, nevertheless Aelian relates of a young child who of old had taken a gold plate from the crown of the goddess Diana: because, when afterwards there were set before him dolls and other little things (in which little children delight), he chose the plate again, he was condemned by the Athenians to death n.

notes.citation: Digest 48.13 (Ad legem Iuliam peculatus et de sacrilegis et de residuis), ll. 1, 4, 6 and 9 (the vulgate numbering of the title differs from the modern); Decretum, C. 17 q. 4, c. 20 Si quis contumax and c. 21 Quisquis [inventus]
notes.original: l. i. l. iiij. l. vj. l. ix. D. ad l. Iul. peculat. c. ſi quis contumax c. quiſ quis. xvij. q. iiij.
notes.gloss: D. 48.13 is the Roman law of sacrilege as theft of sacred things; C. 17 q. 4 the Decretum's treatment of sacrilege and the violation of churches.

notes.citation: The Gloss on c. Sacrilegium (the gloss's definition: sacrilegium committitur auferendo sacrum de sacro, vel non sacrum de sacro, sive sacrum de non sacro), printed as C. 16 q. 3 (or q. 4 — the two readings of the print); the sacrilege canons stand in C. 17 q. 4, where note a cites them, and the print's xvj. is probably xvij.; c. Si quis contumax, already cited at {a}
notes.original: Gloſe. c. ſa crilegium. xvj. q. iij. c. ſi quis contumax. ia allegué.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 23 q. 5, c. 35 Si vos (on the Donatists' rebaptizing, called sacrilege)
notes.original: c. ſi vos xxiij. q. v.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 17 q. 4, c. Si quis contumax, cited above at {a}
notes.original: c. ſi quis cõtumax. prealle gué.
notes.gloss: The canon on violence done to clerics and to churches.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 26 q. 2 (the causa on divination and sorcery), c. 6 Illud [quod est], toward the end
notes.original: c. illud. ſur la fin. xxvi. q. ij.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 1 q. 3 (on simony), c. 1 Audivimus (Gregory; the print's q. ij. is wrong — no Audivimus stands in q. 2)
Code 9.29 (De crimine sacrilegii), l. 2 (C. 9.29.2, Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius)
notes.original: l. ij. C. de cri. ſacrileg.
notes.gloss: Disputare de principali iudicio non oportet: sacrilegii enim instar est dubitare, an is dignus sit, quem elegerit imperator — it is in the nature of sacrilege to doubt whether the man the emperor has chosen is worthy.

notes.citation: Pseudo-Sallust, Invective against Cicero (In M. Tullium Ciceronem invectiva), c. 2
notes.gloss: uxor sacrilega ac periuriis delibuta — "a wife sacrilegious and steeped in perjuries".

notes.citation: Plutarch, Life of Cicero, c. 41 (the divorce of Terentia)
notes.original: Plutarque en la vie de Ciceron.
notes.gloss: Plutarch gives Terentia's neglect of Cicero during the civil war, not her depravity, as the ground; the print's Plutarqne is a turned sort.

notes.citation: Code 9.9 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis et de stupro), l. Quamvis (C. 9.9.29 = vulgate 9.9.30, Constantine), with the print's la ij., which is obscure (perhaps l. ij., a second law of the title); Decretum, C. 11 q. 3 c. 77 (Non solum ille reus est, qui falsum de alio profert), with Gratian's dictum that follows it: Contingit aliquando, ut adulter sententiam pro sacrilegio reportet — the adulterer sentenced as a sacrilegus, which is Coras's point
notes.original: l. quamuis. la ij. C. de adult. c. non ſolũ. xi. q. iij.
notes.gloss: C. 9.9.29: sacrilegos autem nuptiarum gladio puniri oportet — the sacrilegious violators of marriage are to be punished with the sword; this is the text that makes adultery "sacrilege" and so carries Coras's whole annotation.

notes.citation: Digest 48.13 (Ad legem Iuliam peculatus), l. Sacrilegii (D. 48.13.7 = vulgate 48.13.6, Ulpian)
notes.original: l. ſacrilegij. D. ad l. Iuli. pecul.
notes.gloss: The governor fixes the penalty of sacrilege according to the person, the thing, the time, age and sex: Ulpian knows of many condemned to the beasts, some burned alive (nonnullos etiam vivos exussisse), others hanged on the fork.

notes.citation: Digest 4.4 (De minoribus viginti quinque annis), l. Auxilium, § In delictis (D. 4.4.9.2, Ulpian); l. Sacrilegii, as at {l}
notes.original: l. auxilium. P. in dailect. D. de mino. l. ſacrilegij. alleg.
notes.gloss: In delictis autem minor annis viginti quinque non meretur in integrum restitutionem … nisi quatenus interdum miseratio aetatis ad mediocrem poenam iudicem produxerit — a minor has no restitution for his delicts, save that pity for his age may sometimes lead the judge to a moderate penalty. The print's dailect. is delict.

notes.original: Aelian au liure v de var. hiſtor. c. xvi
notes.gloss: The boy who took a gold leaf from the crown of Artemis; offered the leaf again among knucklebones and toys, he chose the leaf, and the Athenians put him to death as a sacrilegious person.
